title: Hydrocarbons
tagline: Alkanes, alkenes, alkynes and arenes: preparation, properties and the orientation of substitution in benzene.

overview.intro: Hydrocarbons are compounds of carbon and hydrogen only, and they are the feedstock from which the rest of organic chemistry is built. This unit classifies them and then treats each family in turn: the alkanes, with their free-radical substitution and their conformations; the alkenes, with Markovnikov addition, the peroxide effect and ozonolysis; the alkynes, with their unexpectedly acidic terminal hydrogen; and the aromatic hydrocarbons, whose stability and electrophilic substitution behaviour follow from resonance and aromaticity. The unit closes with the carcinogenicity and toxicity of certain hydrocarbons, the practical health context of the whole family.

learningOutcomes: Prepare and characterise alkanes, alkenes, alkynes and aromatic hydrocarbons by the standard laboratory methods.
Explain the conformations of ethane and the free-radical mechanism of halogenation of alkanes.
Apply Markovnikov's rule and the peroxide (Kharasch) effect to addition reactions, and use ozonolysis to locate a double bond.
Describe resonance and aromaticity in benzene, predict the orientation of electrophilic substitution, and state the health hazards of hydrocarbons.
Write the initiation, propagation and termination steps of the free-radical chlorination of methane and explain why the reaction gives a mixture of products rather than chloromethane alone.

blocks.text: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CnH2n+2 and only single bonds, so they are relatively unreactive — their common name, paraffins, comes from the Latin for "little affinity". They are prepared in the laboratory by hydrogenating the corresponding alkene or alkyne over a nickel catalyst at about 453 K, by the reduction of an alkyl halide with zinc and dilute acid or with lithium aluminium hydride, by the Wurtz reaction in which two molecules of an alkyl halide couple in dry ether with sodium, and by decarboxylation of the sodium salt of a carboxylic acid with soda-lime, which removes one carbon atom from the chain. Kolbe's electrolytic method gives the same result from the sodium salts of the acid, discharging the carboxylate anode to give the alkyl radical.

The properties of alkanes follow from their structure. They burn in excess oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water with a luminous flame, they undergo substitution by halogens in the presence of sunlight, and they are resistant to most reagents at room temperature. Halogenation proceeds by a free-radical chain mechanism with three stages: initiation, in which ultraviolet light homolytically splits chlorine into two radicals; propagation, in which a chlorine radical abstracts a hydrogen atom from methane to give a methyl radical that attacks another chlorine molecule, repeating the cycle; and termination, in which any two radicals combine, ending the chain. The selectivity of bromination over chlorination follows from the relative stability of the abstracted radical and the endothermicity of the first propagation step.

Because rotation about the carbon-carbon single bond is not completely free, ethane exists as conformations. In the eclipsed conformation the C–H bonds on adjacent carbons line up, maximising repulsion and giving the highest energy, while in the staggered conformation they are 60° apart, minimising repulsion and giving the lowest energy; the difference is only about 12 kJ mol⁻¹, so molecules interconvert millions of times a second and the two cannot be separated. Newman projections show the molecule along the C–C bond with the near carbon as a circle and its three bonds meeting at the centre. In butane, the anti conformation with the two methyl groups 180° apart is the most stable of the four, while the totally eclipsed form, with the methyl groups superimposed, is the least stable.

items.text: Give the equations for the preparation of propane by the Wurtz reaction using a mixture of halides, and by the decarboxylation of a sodium carboxylate.
items.note: Wurtz with a mixture: CH₃Br + CH₃CH₂Br + 2Na →(dry ether) CH₃CH₂CH₃ + NaBr + NaBr, coupling a one-carbon and a two-carbon fragment to give propane (a drawback of the method is that three coupling products are possible). Decarboxylation removes one carbon: CH₃CH₂CH₂COONa + NaOH →(CaO, Δ) CH₃CH₂CH₃ + Na₂CO₃, so the salt of butanoic acid gives propane, while the salt of ethanoic acid would give methane.

items.text: Write the equations for the free-radical chlorination of methane, labelling the initiation, propagation and termination steps, and state why the reaction does not stop after one substitution.
items.note: Initiation: Cl₂ →(UV) 2Cl•. A chlorine molecule absorbs ultraviolet light and undergoes homolytic fission, producing two chlorine radicals each with an unpaired electron. Propagation: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + CH₃•, and CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•. In the first propagation step a chlorine radical abstracts a hydrogen atom from methane, leaving a methyl radical and a molecule of hydrogen chloride; in the second the methyl radical attacks a chlorine molecule, regenerating the chlorine radical. Because the chlorine radical is regenerated, the propagation cycle repeats until reactants are used up or radicals are destroyed. Termination: two radicals combine in a number of ways, for example Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂, CH₃• + Cl• → CH₃Cl, or CH₃• + CH₃• → C₂H₆. The presence of ethane (C₂H₆) as a product is the expected side product from the termination step, and dichloromethane, chloroform and carbon tetrachloride form if the reaction is not controlled, which is why chlorination gives a mixture of products rather than a single compound.

blocks.text: Alkenes contain a carbon-carbon double bond and have the general formula CnH2n. They are prepared by the dehydrohalogenation of alkyl halides with alcoholic potassium hydroxide, which removes a hydrogen halide and follows Saytzeff's rule to give the more substituted (more stable) alkene as the major product, and by the dehydration of alcohols with concentrated sulphuric acid at about 443 K. Because the two carbons of the double bond cannot rotate freely, alkenes show geometrical isomerism: but-2-ene exists as cis and trans forms with different boiling points, and when three different groups are attached to each double-bonded carbon the E-Z notation is used, assigning priorities by atomic number and comparing the two high-priority groups.

The characteristic reactions of alkenes are electrophilic additions. With hydrogen halides the hydrogen adds to the carbon that already carries more hydrogen atoms — Markovnikov's rule — because the reaction passes through the more stable carbocation intermediate: propene with HBr gives 2-bromopropane, not 1-bromopropane. The rule has one famous exception: in the presence of peroxide the same addition gives the anti-Markovnikov product, because the mechanism turns free-radical. A bromine radical adds to the terminal CH₂ carbon so that the more stable secondary carbon radical forms, and that radical then abstracts hydrogen from HBr to give 1-bromopropane while regenerating the bromine radical. The peroxide effect is observed only with HBr: with HCl the first propagation step is endothermic and with HI the second is endothermic, so neither chain can propagate. Alkenes also decolourise bromine water, the standard test for unsaturation, and undergo hydration to alcohols, halogenation to vicinal dihalides and hydrogenation to alkanes.

Ozonolysis locates the position of a double bond. The alkene is treated with ozone at low temperature and the ozonide is then reduced with zinc and water (or dimethyl sulphide), cleaving the double bond and giving a carbonyl compound on each side: ethene gives two molecules of methanal, but-2-ene gives two molecules of ethanal, and pent-2-ene gives ethanal and propanal. Working backwards, the carbonyl products reveal where the double bond was, which makes ozonolysis the standard structure-determining reaction of alkenes.

items.text: What are the products of ozonolysis of pent-2-ene followed by reductive work-up?
items.note: The double bond of CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₃ is cleaved completely: the two-carbon fragment becomes ethanal, CH₃CHO, and the three-carbon fragment becomes propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO. Zinc and water reduce the ozonide without over-oxidising the aldehydes, so both carbonyl products are isolated and their chain lengths reveal exactly where the double bond stood.

items.text: Give the major product of the addition of HBr to propene in the presence of peroxide.
items.note: Anti-Markovnikov addition gives 1-bromopropane, CH₃CH₂CH₂Br. Without peroxide the ionic route through the more stable secondary carbocation would give 2-bromopropane instead, so the presence or absence of peroxide reverses the regiochemistry of the same overall addition.

blocks.text: Alkynes contain a carbon-carbon triple bond, one sigma and two pi bonds, and are linear at the triple bond because each carbon is sp hybridised. They are prepared by the double dehydrohalogenation of a vicinal or geminal dihalide with two equivalents of sodamide in liquid ammonia, and by the reaction of an alkyl halide with sodium acetylide — a method that extends the chain by two carbons from a terminal alkyne. Addition occurs in stages: one equivalent of bromine or hydrogen halide gives the alkene, two equivalents give the fully saturated product, and hydration over a mercury(II) salt follows Markovnikov's rule to give an enol that immediately tautomerises to a ketone — acetylene itself gives ethanal, while propyne gives propanone.

The most distinctive property of terminal alkynes is their acidity. The hydrogen is attached to an sp-hybridised carbon, and since an sp orbital has 50% s character it holds the bonding pair closer to the carbon than an sp² or sp³ orbital does, stabilising the resulting carbanion. Consequently ethyne with a pKa near 25 is acidic enough to be deprotonated by sodium amide, and the acetylide ion reacts with ammoniacal silver nitrate to give a white precipitate of silver ethynide or with ammoniacal cuprous chloride to give a red precipitate of copper(I) ethynide — both classical tests that distinguish a terminal alkyne from an alkene or an internal alkyne. This acidity is also synthetic: the acetylide ion is a nucleophile that extends carbon chains in a controlled way.

learn.title: Aromatic hydrocarbons: benzene, resonance and substitution

blocks.text: Benzene, C₆H₆, is the prototype aromatic compound. Its structure cannot be represented by a single Lewis formula: two Kekulé structures with alternating double bonds differ only in the position of the π electrons, and the real molecule is their hybrid, in which all six carbon-carbon bonds are identical at 139 pm, between a single bond (154 pm) and a double bond (134 pm), and all twelve C–H bonds lie in one plane with 120° angles. The six p electrons are delocalised around the ring in a π electron cloud above and below the plane, which gives benzene the extra stabilisation called resonance energy or delocalisation energy and makes it far less reactive towards addition than an ordinary alkene: addition would destroy the aromatic system, whereas substitution replaces a hydrogen and preserves it.

Benzene and its homologues are prepared industrially by the catalytic reforming of fractions of petroleum over platinum at about 773 K, and in the laboratory by passing benzene vapour over heated zinc dust to reduce it to cyclohexane or by the Clemmensen reduction of acetophenone. Their characteristic reactions are electrophilic substitution, in which the reagent is generated as a strong electrophile and attacks the ring: nitration with concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids at 328-333 K gives nitrobenzene through the nitronium ion NO₂⁺; sulphonation with fuming sulphuric acid gives benzenesulphonic acid; halogenation with a halogen and a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeCl₃ gives halobenzene; Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation use an alkyl or acyl halide with aluminium chloride; and the Kolbe reaction and Gattermann reaction introduce the carboxyl and formyl groups respectively.

Substituents already on the ring decide where the next group goes, through resonance and inductive effects. Activating, ortho- and para-directing groups — -OH, -NH₂, -CH₃ and -OR — donate electron density into the ring (by resonance or hyperconjugation), making it more reactive than benzene and stabilising the intermediate carbocation most when attack occurs at the ortho or para position. Deactivating, meta-directing groups — -NO₂, -CN, -CHO, -COOH and -SO₃H — withdraw electron density, making the ring less reactive, and the meta position is least destabilised. Halogens are the important exception: they are deactivating by the −I effect yet ortho- and para-directing because their lone pairs can still donate by resonance.

Not all hydrocarbons are benign. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons containing several fused benzene rings — benzopyrene formed when organic matter burns incompletely, 3-methylcholanthrene and dibenz[a,h]anthracene — are carcinogenic: they are metabolised in the body to diol epoxides that bind to DNA, damage the bases and cause mutations that may start a tumour. These compounds are present in coal tar, in the soot of incomplete combustion, in cigarette smoke and in charred food. Chronic exposure to benzene itself causes bone-marrow damage and leukaemia, which is why its use as a solvent is controlled. The practical conclusions are straightforward: avoid breathing fumes of any hydrocarbon, do not heat organic compounds over a naked flame unless the procedure calls for it, and work with benzene and its derivatives only with proper ventilation.

items: Alkanes are saturated and relatively inert; their main reaction is free-radical halogenation in sunlight.
Saytzeff's rule: dehydrohalogenation gives the more substituted alkene as the major product.
Markovnikov addition goes through the more stable carbocation; the peroxide effect with HBr gives the anti-Markovnikov product.
Terminal alkynes are acidic because the C–H bond uses an sp orbital; they give white and red precipitates with ammoniacal silver and copper salts.
Benzene undergoes substitution, not addition, to preserve its aromatic sextet.
Ortho-para directors activate the ring except halogens, which deactivate yet still direct ortho-para.
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons such as benzopyrene are carcinogenic; benzene exposure damages bone marrow.

figures.description: Two Newman projections side by side: the eclipsed form, with the front C–H bonds exactly covering the back ones, marked high energy; and the staggered form with the back bonds halfway between the front ones, marked lowest energy. Beside them a cosine-shaped energy curve against the C–C dihedral angle, with a peak at 0° labelled eclipsed and a trough at 60° labelled staggered, and the barrier marked as 12 kJ mol⁻¹.
labels: Front carbon drawn as a point, back as a circle
Rotation barrier of only 12 kJ mol⁻¹

figures.caption: Figure: Electrophilic substitution in benzene — nitration
figures.description: A two-step diagram: first, HNO₃ is protonated by H₂SO₄ and loses water to generate the linear nitronium ion O=N=O⁺, drawn with its resonance structures; second, the nitronium ion approaches the electron-rich π cloud of the ring, an arrow shows a pair of π electrons attacking the nitrogen to give a positively charged intermediate (sigma complex) with the charge delocalised over three ring positions, followed by loss of H⁺ to restore the aromatic ring and give nitrobenzene.
labels: Loss of H⁺ restores the aromatic sextet

keyPoints: Alkanes: CnH2n+2, prepared by hydrogenation, Wurtz, decarboxylation and reduction.
Halogenation of alkanes is a free-radical chain: initiation, propagation and termination.
Ethane exists as eclipsed and staggered conformations differing by 12 kJ mol⁻¹; butane has anti and gauche forms.
Alkenes: CnH2n, prepared by dehydrohalogenation (Saytzeff product) and dehydration of alcohols.
Markovnikov addition passes through the more stable carbocation; peroxide reverses the orientation for HBr only.
Ozonolysis cleaves a double bond to carbonyl compounds and so reveals its position.
Terminal alkynes are acidic (sp carbon) and give white Ag and red Cu precipitates with ammoniacal salts.
Benzene has six equivalent 139 pm bonds and a delocalised π sextet, giving resonance stabilisation.
Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution: nitration, sulphonation, halogenation, Friedel-Crafts reactions.
Ortho-para directors donate density (OH, NH₂, CH₃, halogens); meta directors withdraw it (NO₂, CN, CHO).
examFocus: This 10-mark unit carries a mechanism question almost every year: write the steps of free-radical substitution or electrophilic substitution with curved arrows.
Predicting the products of addition with and without peroxide, and identifying the carbonyl products of ozonolysis, are standard application questions.
Name reactions — Wurtz, Kolbe, Markovnikov, Friedel-Crafts, Clemmensen — must be learned with their reagents and one equation each.

vocabulary.meaning: A spatial arrangement obtained by rotation about a single bond, interconvertible without breaking bonds.
In addition to an unsymmetrical alkene the hydrogen adds to the carbon already bearing more hydrogen atoms.
Cleavage of a double bond by ozone followed by reduction to give carbonyl products.
The extra stabilisation of a planar, fully conjugated ring with 4n+2 π electrons — six for benzene.
Replacement of a ring hydrogen by an electrophile, preserving the aromatic system.
Dehydrohalogenation favours the more substituted, more stable alkene.
A substance that promotes the formation of cancer, such as benzopyrene from incomplete combustion.

questions.prompt: The major product of the reaction of propene with HBr in the presence of peroxide is:
questions.explanation: With peroxide the reaction follows a free-radical chain rather than the ionic Markovnikov route. The bromine radical adds to the terminal carbon so that the secondary carbon radical forms, and hydrogen abstraction then gives 1-bromopropane — the anti-Markovnikov orientation known as the Kharasch or peroxide effect.

questions.prompt: When propyne is hydrated in the presence of a mercuric sulphate catalyst, the product formed is:
questions.explanation: Hydration follows Markovnikov orientation, giving the enol CH₃C(OH)=CH₂, which immediately tautomerises to the more stable ketone propanone, CH₃COCH₃. Propanal would require anti-Markovnikov hydration, which this reagent does not give.

questions.prompt: Which reagent distinguishes a terminal alkyne from an alkene?
questions.explanation: The hydrogen on an sp-hybridised terminal carbon is acidic enough to be removed by the base in ammoniacal silver nitrate, precipitating the white silver acetylide. Both alkene and terminal alkyne decolourise bromine water and permanganate, and both add hydrogen, so only the ammoniacal silver salt distinguishes them.

questions.prompt: The carbon-carbon bond length in benzene compared with C–C (154 pm) and C=C (134 pm) is:
options: about 139 pm, identical for all six bonds
questions.answer: about 139 pm, identical for all six bonds
questions.explanation: Delocalisation makes all six carbon-carbon bonds identical, with a length intermediate between single and double, about 139 pm. If the Kekulé structures were correct as written the ring would have two distinct bond lengths, which experiment does not observe.

questions.prompt: The general formula of the alkenes is __________.
questions.explanation: Alkenes contain one carbon-carbon double bond, which removes two hydrogens from the corresponding alkane, giving CnH2n with n ≥ 2; the simplest member is ethene, C₂H₄.

questions.prompt: The laboratory preparation of ethyne from calcium carbide and water requires __________.
questions.explanation: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → C₂H₂ + Ca(OH)₂ proceeds vigorously at room temperature without any catalyst, so the apparatus is designed to control the addition of water rather than to supply heat; a dropping funnel or Kipp arrangement delivers the water slowly and the gas is collected over water.

questions.prompt: State the three stages of the free-radical chlorination of methane and give one equation for each stage.
questions.answer: Initiation: ultraviolet light homolytically splits chlorine, Cl₂ →(hv) 2Cl•, generating the radicals that start the chain. Propagation: a chlorine atom abstracts a hydrogen, CH₄ + Cl• → CH₃• + HCl, and the methyl radical attacks a chlorine molecule, CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•, regenerating the chlorine atom so the cycle repeats. Termination: any two radicals combine and end the chain, for example CH₃• + CH₃• → C₂H₆ or Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂. Because propagation regenerates the radical, a single initiation event can lead to many thousands of substitutions.
questions.explanation: The three stages must be named and each shown with an equation, since the chain-carrying role of the propagating radical is what makes the reaction self-sustaining.

questions.prompt: Explain why benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition, even though it is unsaturated.
questions.answer: Benzene is unsaturated in the sense of having a low hydrogen-to-carbon ratio, but its six π electrons are delocalised over the whole ring, giving resonance stabilisation of about 150 kJ mol⁻¹. An addition reaction would break the delocalisation and destroy this aromatic stabilisation, costing far more energy than it gains. Substitution replaces a ring hydrogen while restoring the fully aromatic system at the end, so the stabilisation is retained. The intermediate of substitution does lose aromaticity temporarily, but it regains it on loss of H⁺, whereas an addition product cannot regain it at all.
questions.explanation: Full marks require the concept of aromatic stabilisation (resonance energy) as the energetic reason, not merely the observation that substitution occurs.

questions.prompt: Describe the laboratory preparation of ethyne, write the equation, and explain why the gas is passed through a copper sulphate solution before it is collected.
questions.answer: Ethyne is prepared by dropping water onto calcium carbide: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → C₂H₂ + Ca(OH)₂ + heat. The apparatus delivers the gas as it is needed, since the reaction is vigorous, and the ethyne is collected over water because it is only slightly soluble. The crude gas contains impurities of hydrogen sulphide and phosphine that arise from calcium phosphide and calcium sulphide present in the technical carbide, and these impurities would interfere with subsequent reactions — phosphine in particular can form explosive copper compounds. Washing the gas through a solution of copper sulphate or through sodium hydroxide removes them: H₂S reacts to give copper sulphide and phosphine is absorbed, leaving pure ethyne ready for use. The gas is then dried if a dry sample is required.
questions.explanation: The impurity removal step is what earns the extra marks: naming hydrogen sulphide and phosphine and giving the reason for removing them shows understanding beyond memorising the equation.

questions.prompt: An aromatic compound C₆H₆ on reaction with chlorine in the presence of a ferric chloride catalyst gives C₆H₅Cl. State the type of mechanism involved, outline its three steps, and explain why the compound does not add chlorine as an alkene would. Predict the product if the ring carried a -CH₃ group instead of a hydrogen.
questions.answer: The reaction is electrophilic aromatic substitution. Step 1, generation of the electrophile: Cl₂ is polarised by the Lewis acid catalyst, Cl₂ + FeCl₃ → Cl⁺ + FeCl₄⁻, producing a chloronium electrophile. Step 2, attack on the ring: a pair of π electrons from benzene attacks Cl⁺, forming a sigma complex (arenium ion) in which the positive charge is delocalised over three ring carbons and aromaticity is temporarily lost. Step 3, restoration of aromaticity: FeCl₄⁻ abstracts a proton from the sp³ carbon of the sigma complex, regenerating FeCl₃ and HCl and restoring the delocalised sextet, giving chlorobenzene. Benzene does not add chlorine because addition would permanently destroy the aromatic resonance stabilisation of about 150 kJ mol⁻¹; substitution retains it, so the substitution pathway is far lower in energy overall. If the ring carries a methyl group, toluene is formed, and the methyl group is an ortho-para directing activator by hyperconjugation and the +I effect, so the products are a mixture of 2-chlorotoluene and 4-chlorotoluene with the para isomer usually predominant because of steric hindrance at the ortho position.
questions.explanation: The mechanism must be written with the catalyst regenerated in the final step and the sigma complex named; the orientation prediction then follows directly from the electronic effect of the existing substituent.
